opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's great to be here.

For me, this goes back a long way. I've spent most of my career thinking about visual intelligence, starting with object recognition and the ImageNet days, and later with my students working on scene understanding, visual relationships, and connecting vision and language. Justin was one of those students. He did some wonderful work in my lab on things like image captioning, scene graphs, and style transfer, and we've stayed close collaborators and friends ever since.

Over the past several years, especially as large language models took off, we kept coming back to the same feeling: language is incredibly powerful, but it isn't the whole story of intelligence. If you look at evolution, animals were perceiving, moving, and acting in a three-dimensional world for hundreds of millions of years before anything like language appeared. Seeing, understanding the structure of space, and interacting with it is a much more fundamental layer. I'd call that spatial intelligence, and I believe it's one of the most important unsolved problems in AI.

What made the timing feel right was the convergence of several things. Generative models had gotten remarkably good. We'd seen big advances in 3D representations, neural rendering, and reconstruction. And compute and data had reached a scale where you could seriously imagine models that don't just label pixels or produce flat images, but actually understand and generate full 3D worlds that are consistent, persistent, and that you can reason about and act within.

Justin and I talked a lot about it, and we realized this wasn't something to do as a side project or a single paper. It required a dedicated team bringing together people from computer vision, graphics, and machine learning, with the resources to push on it at scale. That's really why we started World Labs. We think world models are the next frontier, and that getting spatial intelligence right will unlock applications in creativity and design, robotics, simulation, and eventually how we interact with both the physical and virtual worlds.

And honestly, it's a problem we both just find deeply exciting. When you've spent your life asking how we see and understand the world, building machines that can do it too is about the most compelling thing you could work on.

r001.rationale: The response says language is not the whole story of intelligence and presents spatial intelligence and world models as a fundamental next frontier for AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, for me it really comes from a very long-standing conviction about what intelligence actually is. I've spent most of my career on visual intelligence, and the deeper I went, the more I came to believe that language is not the whole story. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years developing perception and the ability to act in a three-dimensional world before anything like language showed up. That's what I've been calling spatial intelligence, and I think it's a fundamental pillar of intelligence, not a side feature.

So when the generative AI wave hit, I was of course excited by what language models could do, but I also felt there was a gap. Most of what humans and animals do, from understanding a scene to picking up a cup to navigating a room, is deeply spatial. If we want AI that can really understand and interact with the world, whether that's for creativity, for robotics, for science, we need models that understand 3D, that understand physics and geometry, not just the statistics of text.

Justin and I have known each other since he was my student at Stanford, and he was one of the earliest people pushing hard on generative visual work and then on 3D and neural rendering. We'd been talking for years about this, and around 2023 the ingredients started to line up: the compute, the data, the architectural advances. It felt like one of those moments where a hard problem suddenly becomes tractable, and if you believe in it, you have to go after it.

The other piece was that I felt this had to be done with the focus and resources of a company. It's not a single paper. It's a multi-year systems effort that needs engineering, infrastructure, and a team that wakes up every day thinking only about this. So we committed, and World Labs became that vehicle for building world models and what I hope will be the next frontier of AI.

r001.rationale: The response says language models leave a gap and argues AI development needs world models that understand 3D, physics, and geometry, framing spatial intelligence as a fundamental pillar beyond language.

astra-6.text:
For me, it was the conviction that intelligence goes beyond language. So much of what we do depends on understanding the world in three dimensions: how things are arranged, how they move, and how our own actions change what happens next. Even something as ordinary as picking up a cup involves a tremendous amount of spatial intelligence.

Justin and I share a deep interest in that problem. Computer vision has made extraordinary progress, but recognizing what is in an image is only part of the challenge. We want systems that can understand the underlying world, imagine different possibilities, and reason about what happens when you interact with it.

What made us commit was the sense that this was becoming a problem we could make real progress on. The advances in generative models opened up a way to move from perceiving images toward generating and understanding worlds. That felt like a compelling next step, both scientifically and in terms of what it could enable people to create. World Labs was our way of committing fully to that direction.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence goes beyond language and describes building systems that understand, imagine, and reason about three-dimensional worlds.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was a convergence of a long-standing scientific passion and a sense that the technology was ready for a new chapter. I’ve spent much of my career thinking about visual intelligence. Seeing is not just recognizing an object or describing an image. It’s understanding a world with structure, space, and physical relationships—and being able to act in it.

Justin and I shared that conviction. Language is incredibly powerful, but so much of human intelligence comes from interacting with the three-dimensional world. We wanted to pursue models that could understand and generate that world, going beyond individual images to something more spatially coherent.

The excitement was both scientific and practical: could we make progress on this fundamental piece of intelligence and put it into the hands of people who create? Founding World Labs was our way of committing fully to that question.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language’s limits with the goal of building models that understand and generate the three-dimensional world, presenting spatial intelligence as a direction beyond language models.
